/-!
# Erdős Problem 200

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/200](https://www.erdosproblems.com/200)
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter Real

namespace Erdos200

/--
The length of the longest arithmetic progression of primes in $\{1,\ldots,n\}$.
-/
noncomputable def longestPrimeArithmeticProgressions (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sSup {(k : ℕ) | ∃ s ⊆ Set.Icc 1 n, s.IsAPOfLength k ∧ ∀ m ∈ s, m.Prime}

/--
Does the longest arithmetic progression of primes in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ have length $o(\log N)$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_200 : answer(sorry) ↔
    (fun n => (longestPrimeArithmeticProgressions n : ℝ)) =o[atTop] (fun n => log n) := by
  sorry

/--
It follows from the prime number theorem that such a progression has length $\leq(1+o(1))\log N$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_200.variants.upper : ∃ (o : ℕ → ℝ) (_ : o =o[atTop] (1 : ℕ → ℝ)),
    ∀ n, longestPrimeArithmeticProgressions n ≤ (1 + o n) * log n := by
  sorry

end Erdos200

reformulations.difference: The source states the asymptotic upper bound L(N) ≤ (1+o(1)) log N. Lean requires the inequality for every natural n, rather than merely eventually, using an existential error function o =o[atTop] 1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: These formulations are equivalent. An all-n bound implies an eventual bound. Conversely, given an eventual bound, retain its error function beyond a cutoff and set it to L(n)/log n − 1 at the finitely many exceptional n ≥ 2. The logarithm is positive there, so this makes the inequality an equality. At n = 0 and n = 1, both L(n) and log n are zero, so the bound holds automatically. Finite modifications preserve o(1). The all-n/eventual equivalence, the boundary values, and the interpretation of o =o 1 as convergence to zero were proved in /workspace/review/scratch.lean.
